markscheme_points.text: force per unit length; force per unit current; length / current perpendicular to field
markscheme_points.guidance: 1 mark for any two points, 2 marks for all three points

hints: Hint 1: Think about what experiment defines $B$ - the force felt by a small current-carrying wire placed in the field. What three quantities must the force depend on?
Hint 2: Remember that the force is maximum only for one special orientation of wire and field. What orientation gives the definition of one tesla?
parts.proper_answer: Magnetic flux density is the force per unit current per unit length on a conductor placed perpendicular to the field, $B = F/IL$ for $\sin 90^{\circ} = 1$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link B to force on a current**
You already know a magnet pushes on a wire carrying current. $B$ is defined to make that quantitative. Think of a straight wire of length $L$ carrying current $I$ in a field $B$. The general force is $F = BIL\sin\theta$.

Step 2: **Pick the maximum-force condition**
The definition uses $\theta = 90^{\circ}$, so the length is perpendicular to the field and $\sin\theta = 1$. Then $$B = \frac{F}{IL}$$ This says $1\text{ T}$ is $1\text{ N}$ per ampere per metre when perpendicular.

parts.label: (b)
(b)(i)
parts.text: State the direction of the magnetic field.
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 6.1 - at X the electrons move right but are forced downward into a clockwise curve. Remember electrons carry negative charge, so conventional current points opposite to their velocity. Which way must $B$ point to give a downward force?
parts.proper_answer: Into the plane of the page.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use Fleming's left-hand rule carefully**
At X velocity $v$ is to the right and the magnetic force $F$ must be downward to start the clockwise loop. For a positive charge, $F$ is given by $v$ cross $B$. For an electron the charge is negative, so conventional current $I$ is to the left.

Step 2: **Find B direction**
Point left-hand First finger for $B$, Second finger for current to the left, thumb for force down. This only works if the First finger points into the page. So $B$ is directed into the page.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Show that the magnitude of the force exerted on each electron by the magnetic field is $1.3 \times 10^{-14}\text{ N}$.
hints: Hint 1: The electrons enter at right angles to the uniform field, so the force is maximum. Check the data: what is the charge magnitude of one electron and what is $4.8\text{ mT}$ in tesla?
Hint 2: Combine $B$, $q$ and $v$ multiplicatively to get the magnitude, then round to two significant figures to show the given value.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the moving-charge force law**
A charge $q$ moving perpendicular to $B$ feels $$F = Bqv$$ Here $q = e = 1.60\times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, $B = 4.8\text{ mT} = 4.8\times 10^{-3}\text{ T}$, $v = 1.7\times 10^{7}\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Calculate and show**
$$F = (4.8\times 10^{-3})\times (1.60\times 10^{-19})\times (1.7\times 10^{7})$$ $$F \approx 1.31\times 10^{-14}\text{ N} \approx 1.3\times 10^{-14}\text{ N}$$ This matches the stated value, with force perpendicular to $v$ so speed stays constant.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: On Fig. 6.1, draw an arrow to indicate the direction of the centripetal acceleration of the electron where it enters the magnetic field at point $X$.

markscheme_points.text: arrow at point X pointing down the page

hints: Hint 1: Centripetal acceleration always points to the centre of the circular path. At X the path curves downward into a semi-circle below X - where is the centre relative to X?
parts.proper_answer: Arrow at X pointing vertically down the page, toward the centre of the semi-circular path.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Point to the centre**
Magnetic force provides the centripetal force, so acceleration $a$ is in the same direction as $F$, toward the centre of the circle. At X the centre of the small semi-circle lies directly below X. So draw a short arrow at X straight down the page.

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.text: Use the information in (b)(ii) to calculate the distance $d$ between the path of the electrons entering the magnetic field and the path of the electrons leaving it.
hints: Hint 1: Inside the field the speed is constant but direction changes - this is uniform circular motion. What physical agent supplies the required inward centripetal force?
Hint 2: Equate the magnetic force from (b)(ii) to the circular-motion expression involving $m$, $v$ and $r$, then rearrange to make $r$ the subject before inserting numbers.
Hint 3: Look again at Fig. 6.1 - the distance $d$ spans the full width of the semi-circle. How is $d$ related to the radius $r$ you just found?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Set magnetic force equal to centripetal requirement**
The electron mass is $m = 9.11\times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$. For circular motion: $$F = \frac{mv^{2}}{r}$$ where $F$ is the $1.3\times 10^{-14}\text{ N}$ from (b)(ii).

Step 2: **Solve for radius**
$$r = \frac{mv^{2}}{F} = \frac{(9.11\times 10^{-31})\times (1.7\times 10^{7})^{2}}{1.3\times 10^{-14}}$$ $$r \approx 0.020\text{ m}$$

Step 3: **Convert radius to distance d**
Fig. 6.1 shows a half-circle. The entry and exit paths are separated by one diameter: $$d = 2r \approx 0.040\text{ m}$$

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The electrons in (b) are replaced with positrons that are moving with speed $3.4 \times 10^7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ along the same initial path as the electrons.
The positrons enter the magnetic field at point $X$ on Fig. 6.1.

On Fig. 6.1, draw a line to show the path of the positrons through the magnetic field.

markscheme_points.text: path shows upwards deflection such that the curvature is always anticlockwise within the field
line enters field at X and leaves field at distance $2d$ vertically from X

hints: Hint 1: A positron has the same mass as an electron but opposite (+e) charge and here twice the speed. First decide: with the same $v$ to the right and same $B$ into the page, which way does the force on a positive charge point compared to the electron in Fig. 6.1?
Hint 2: Next think about the size of the circle. With $r = mv/Bq$, how does doubling $v$ with the same $m$, $B$ and $|q|$ change $r$ compared to part (b)?
Hint 3: Combine direction and size to sketch the new semi-circle starting at X. Where will it exit the field edge relative to the old exit distance $d$?
parts.proper_answer: Upward-curving semi-circle starting at X, circular with radius twice that in (b), exiting the field a distance $2d$ above the entry level (diameter $=2d$).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Reverse the deflection direction**
Positron charge is $+e$, opposite to electron. For the same $v$ right and $B$ into page, Fleming's left-hand rule gives force upward, not downward. So the path curves upward from X, always anticlockwise while in the field.

Step 2: **Compare the radius**
For any particle $$r = \frac{mv}{Bq}$$ Positron has same $m$ and $|q|$ as electron, same $B$, but $v = 3.4\times 10^{7}\text{ m s}^{-1} = 2\times 1.7\times 10^{7}\text{ m s}^{-1}$. So $r$ is doubled. The curvature is gentler - larger circle.

Step 3: **Draw the exit point**
Draw a larger upward semi-circle entering at X and leaving the left edge of the field. Its diameter is $2\times r_{new} = 4\times r_{old} = 2d$. So the exit is a vertical distance $2d$ from X, about twice the separation shown for electrons.
